reason: The sources provide multi-site corroboration for dozens of atomic facts detailing the warnings, decoy tactics, fatal ambush, and political fallout.
story: In December 1866, tensions along the Bozeman Trail peaked around Fort Phil Kearny. Captain William J. Fetterman, a decorated Civil War veteran who allegedly boasted he could ride through the entire Sioux nation with eighty men, chafed under Colonel Henry B. Carrington's strictly defensive orders. On December 21, Native warriors attacked a military wood-cutting train. Carrington ordered a relief detachment out, explicitly forbidding pursuit beyond Lodge Trail Ridge, where soldiers would lose sight and support of the fort. Instead of simply rescuing the wagons, Fetterman followed a small group of decoys, including the young warrior Crazy Horse, over the crest. Waiting in ambush were roughly a thousand Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors. Within thirty to forty minutes, Fetterman and all eighty men under his command were encircled and wiped out. The devastating defeat ultimately forced the United States to abandon its forts along the Bozeman Trail.
angle: Ordered strictly not to cross the ridge out of sight of the fort, an arrogant officer took exactly eighty men after a decoy lure—the exact number he had allegedly boasted could ride through the entire Sioux nation—and every single one was killed in under an hour.

claims.claim: The battle took place on December 21, 1866, near Fort Phil Kearny in present-day Wyoming.
The fight occurred during the conflict known as Red Cloud's War.
Fort Phil Kearny was built along the Bozeman Trail to protect travelers and emigrants heading west.
The commander of Fort Phil Kearny was Colonel Henry B. Carrington.
Captain William J. Fetterman was a decorated veteran of the American Civil War.
Fetterman allegedly boasted that with 80 men he could ride through the entire Sioux nation.
The Native force confronting the U.S. Army was an alliance primarily composed of Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors.
On the morning of December 21, 1866, Native warriors attacked a wood train supplying the fort.
Carrington ordered the relief force under no circumstances to pursue the enemy over Lodge Trail Ridge.
Fetterman commanded a relief detachment totaling 81 men, consisting of officers, soldiers, and two civilians.
The two armed civilians who accompanied the detachment were James Wheatley and Isaac Fisher.
A small group of Native decoys that included the young warrior Crazy Horse lured the soldiers into the trap.
Fetterman led his men across Lodge Trail Ridge in pursuit of the decoys, violating Carrington's explicit orders.
An estimated force of at least 1,000 Native warriors lay concealed in wait north of the ridge.
The entire command under Fetterman was wiped out, leaving no American survivors.
The combat lasted approximately thirty minutes to an hour before all soldiers were killed.
Captain Tenodor Ten Eyck was sent from the fort with a relief party after firing was heard, but arrived too late to save anyone.
The victorious Native Americans referred to the encounter as the Battle of the Hundred-in-the-Hands or Hundred Slain.
John 'Portugee' Phillips volunteered to ride more than 230 miles through a severe blizzard to carry news of the disaster to Fort Laramie.
Until the Battle of the Little Bighorn a decade later, the Fetterman Fight stood as the U.S. Army's worst defeat on the Great Plains.
Following the disaster, Colonel Carrington was relieved of his command in January 1867.
The U.S. military abandoned Fort Phil Kearny and its other Bozeman Trail forts in 1868.

disputed: Fetterman's alleged quote, 'Give me 80 men and I can ride through the whole Sioux nation,' was published years later by Carrington's wives to defend Carrington's reputation; modern historians question whether Fetterman was truly arrogant or framed as a scapegoat. A script should attribute it: 'according to accounts published by Carrington's family' or 'Fetterman reportedly boasted.'

Whether Captains Fetterman and Brown died by mutual suicide or were killed by warriors; army autopsy reports showed a throat slash on Fetterman, while Lakota oral history credits American Horse with the kill. A script should note: 'some claimed the officers shot each other to avoid capture, though military autopsies and Native accounts contradict this.'

Whether Chief Red Cloud was personally present and participating in the combat or remained at the main camp due to age. A script should attribute: 'accounts differ on whether Red Cloud was present on the field or organized the assault from camp.'

Whether Carrington clearly gave the explicit order not to cross Lodge Trail Ridge, or if Fetterman was executing an offensive pincer movement intended to cut off the retreating raiders. A script should attribute: 'Carrington insisted he ordered Fetterman never to cross the ridge, though later historians suggest the plan may have been an authorized offensive maneuver.'
